clinicalPearls: Abnormal thyroid function tests in acutely or chronically unwell patients who do not have intrinsic thyroid disease
The earliest and most consistent change is a low triiodothyronine (T3), with normal or low thyroid-stimulating hormone
In severe or prolonged illness thyroxine (T4) also falls, and a very low T4 predicts a poor prognosis
It reflects an adaptive response to illness rather than true thyroid dysfunction
Thyroid function testing is best avoided in acutely ill patients unless thyroid disease is genuinely suspected
Thyroid hormone replacement is generally not indicated and testing should be repeated after recovery
reference.pathophysiology: Euthyroid sick syndrome results from illness-induced changes in thyroid hormone metabolism and regulation rather than thyroid gland disease. Reduced peripheral conversion of T4 to active T3 (with shunting toward inactive reverse T3), altered binding proteins, and central downregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis by cytokines and other mediators combine to lower measured hormone levels. This is regarded as an adaptive response to conserve energy during illness, and thyroid function typically normalises as the underlying condition resolves.
additionalDifferentials: Effects of drugs on thyroid tests (for example steroids, dopamine, amiodarone)
additionalInvestigations: Interpretation of thyroid tests in the context of acute illness
Repeat testing after recovery from the acute illness
Review of drugs affecting thyroid tests
Assessment for genuine thyroid disease only where clinically indicated
Correlation with the clinical picture rather than treating numbers
redFlags: A very low thyroxine in critical illness (poor prognostic marker)
Genuine clinical features of thyroid disease
Suspected central hypothyroidism with other pituitary deficits
Diagnostic confusion with amiodarone or other drug effects
reference.prognosis: The thyroid test abnormalities themselves are benign and resolve with recovery; a markedly low thyroxine reflects severe underlying illness and is associated with worse outcomes.
pitfalls: Testing thyroid function unnecessarily in acutely ill patients and misinterpreting the results
Treating the abnormal numbers with thyroid hormone
management: Direct treatment at the underlying acute illness, as the thyroid test changes are adaptive and resolve with recovery
Avoid thyroid hormone replacement, which is generally not indicated and may be harmful
Avoid routine thyroid function testing in acutely ill patients unless intrinsic thyroid disease is genuinely suspected
Review drugs that alter thyroid tests, such as glucocorticoids, dopamine and amiodarone
Repeat thyroid function after recovery to confirm normalisation rather than treating numbers
Recognise a markedly low thyroxine as a marker of illness severity warranting intensive supportive care
